newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Maori ministry warns of racial conflict.
newsitem.headline: NZ Maori ministry warns of racial conflict.

text.p: Social and economic disparities between Maori and non-Maori threaten social order in New Zealand's cities, a government ministry warned the new centre-right coalition on Friday.

Ngatata Love, chief executive of the Maori Development Ministry, said in a briefing paper that under-representation of Maori in mainstream life imposed social and economic costs on all New Zealanders "and has the capacity to produce conflict".

Maori, the original Polynesian settlers of New Zealand who arrived 1,000 years before white Europeans, make up 13 percent of the population and are over-represented in negative health, education, employment and crime statistics.

From cradle to grave and cot death to cancer, Maori suffer higher rates of disease than their fellow New Zealanders and have shorter life expectancy. Maori unemployment, at around 14 percent, is about three times the rate of white New Zealanders.
"The disparities are the major concern of Maori and represent the biggest drain on the nation, and threaten social order in our cities," Love said.

"It is likely that if Maori are disappointed in their expectations of justice, there will be a return to the activism seen in the seventies and early eighties and again following the release of the fiscal envelope."

The previous conservative National party government imposed a NZ$1 billion (US$710 million) "fiscal envelope" for settling historical grievances over land and assets taken from Maori since colonial times.
Maori rejected the ceiling on their claims, and it was dumped as part of last month's coalition deal between the National and New Zealand First parties.
Seven of NZ First's 17 MPs are of Maori descent and policies to address Maori concerns were prominent in the coalition deal.
Love said Maori saw little commitment from government to action on the scale needed to eliminate the disparities.

"These concerns build a picture of injustices done to Maori which threaten cultural and even personal survival. On the Pakeha (European New Zealanders') side are feelings of impatience, guilt, wrongful blame and powerlessness to meet Maori demands.
"While New Zealand has a fair record, the frequency of ethnically-based conflicts overseas warns against complacency."
He said the first priority of the government should be rapid social and economic development for Maori. The second priority should be resolving grievances under the Treaty of Waitangi.

The Treaty, signed between Britain and Maori chiefs last century, ensured British rule and cleared the way for further colonial settlement, while granting Maori British citizenship and rights to their lands, resources and "treasures".

In a separate development on Friday, the British-based Privy Council, New Zealand's highest court, quashed a Court of Appeal decision allowing urban Maori with no tribal links to benefit from the settlement of historical grievances.

Eighty percent of Maori live in cities and many do not maintain tribal links. In his briefing, Love said the issue of how to compensate urban Maori and ensure they had an equal say in the settlement of claims was critical and must be resolved.
